title: The PE Teacher
subtitle: Five years of getting children to move, and what she has learned about how to do it.
description: A B1 reading and listening text about a physical education teacher, written with a clear tense scheme — present perfect for experience, past simple for events, future for plans — with vocabulary and comprehension exercises.
passage: Caroline has taught physical education at the same primary school for five years, and in that time she has worked out something that took her a while to accept: most children do not dislike exercise. They dislike being bad at it in front of other people. Once she understood that, she changed how she taught.

The first thing she did was stop picking teams the old way. Standing two children at the front to choose their friends in order tells every child exactly where they rank, and the ones picked last had usually stopped trying before the game began. Now she divides the class herself, differently every week, and nobody knows who is supposed to be the good one.

She has introduced a lot of games over the years — tag, small-sided soccer, relays with teams too short to hide in. She has brought in hoops and balls of different sizes, because a child who cannot catch a tennis ball can catch a beach ball and will keep trying. She has used music, which turned out to work far better than she expected: several children who refused to run will dance for twenty minutes without noticing.

Last month she ran a relay race that the whole school still talks about. She set it up so that each team needed a fast runner, a careful one and somebody who could throw, which meant no team could win on speed alone. Three children who had never been picked for anything ended up deciding their races. She has run it twice since.

Not everything has worked. She tried yoga two years ago, hoping it would help the children who arrive at school already anxious, and the first attempt was a failure because she scheduled it straight after lunch when they were at their loudest. She moved it to the end of the day and it has been one of her most popular sessions ever since. She has kept the lesson and thrown away the timetable, which is the sort of adjustment nobody tells you about before you start teaching.

Next week she is running a treasure hunt across the playground. She has hidden the clues already, and she has written them so that each one needs two children to solve it — one has to read and one has to count. In the spring she is planning a swimming day, if the weather is warm enough, and she wants to start a lunchtime fitness club before the end of the year. She has also begun inviting parents to the sports afternoons, which some of them find more intimidating than the children do.

Ask her what the job is actually about and she will not say fitness. She says her aim is that a child leaves her class at eleven still willing to try something they are not yet good at. Everything else, she says, follows from that.

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: Read for what Caroline has learned, not just what she does.

items.prompt: What did Caroline come to accept about children and exercise?
options: That most dislike not exercise itself, but being visibly bad at it in front of others
That most genuinely dislike physical activity
That children enjoy exercise only when they are winning
items.explanation: “They dislike being bad at it in front of other people. Once she understood that, she changed how she taught.”

items.prompt: Why did she stop letting children pick teams?
options: Because it took too long at the start of the lesson
Because it tells every child their rank, and those picked last had already given up
Because the same children always won
items.explanation: The process itself broadcasts the ranking, which does the damage before the game starts.

items.prompt: Why does she use balls of different sizes?
options: To teach different sports in the same lesson
Because a child who cannot catch a tennis ball can catch a beach ball and will keep trying
Because the school could not afford a full set
items.explanation: The adjustment keeps the child in the activity rather than proving they cannot do it.

items.prompt: How did she design the relay race so that it was not decided by speed?
options: She gave slower runners a head start
Each team needed a fast runner, a careful one and someone who could throw
items.explanation: Which is why “three children who had never been picked for anything ended up deciding their races”.

items.prompt: Why did the yoga fail the first time?
options: The children found it too difficult
It was scheduled straight after lunch, when the children were at their loudest
There was not enough space in the hall
items.explanation: The lesson was sound; the timing was wrong. Moving it to the end of the day fixed it.

items.prompt: What does “she has kept the lesson and thrown away the timetable” mean?
options: That she no longer follows any schedule
That she abandoned yoga but kept the idea
That when something failed she changed when it happened rather than dropping the activity
items.explanation: It names the distinction between a bad idea and a badly placed one — “the sort of adjustment nobody tells you about”.

items.prompt: Why does each treasure-hunt clue need two children?
options: To make the hunt last longer
Because each clue requires both reading and counting, so they have to cooperate
Because the playground is too large for one child
items.explanation: “One has to read and one has to count” — the cooperation is designed into the puzzle.

items.prompt: How does Caroline describe the aim of her job?
options: That children leave at eleven still willing to try something they are not yet good at
That every child should reach a basic level of fitness
That children should find a sport they can compete in
items.explanation: She explicitly does not say fitness — “everything else, she says, follows from that”.

exercises.title: Which Tense?
exercises.instructions: Present perfect for experience over a period up to now. Past simple for a finished event at a stated time. Present continuous or going to for a plan.

items.prompt: Caroline ___ at the same school for five years.
items.explanation: “For five years” up to now takes the present perfect. The past simple would mean she no longer teaches there.

items.prompt: Last month she ___ a relay race that the whole school still talks about.
items.explanation: A single finished event at a stated past time — past simple. The source's “had organised” was wrong: a past perfect needs a later past point to sit before.
“Since” ties the period to now, so present perfect — the natural follow-up to a past simple event.

items.prompt: She ___ yoga two years ago, and the first attempt ___ a failure.
items.explanation: “Two years ago” fixes both verbs in finished past time.

items.prompt: It ___ one of her most popular sessions ever since.
items.explanation: A state that began in the past and continues — “ever since” requires the present perfect.

items.prompt: Next week she ___ a treasure hunt, and she ___ the clues already.
items.explanation: Present continuous for a fixed arrangement; present perfect with “already” for preparation completed before now.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the text.

items.statement: Caroline lets the children choose their own teams.
items.explanation: False — she divides the class herself, differently every week, precisely so nobody is ranked.

items.statement: Music worked better than she expected.
items.explanation: True — children who refused to run “will dance for twenty minutes without noticing”.
False — it was moved to the end of the day and has been popular ever since.

items.statement: The swimming day depends on the weather.
items.explanation: True — “in the spring she is planning a swimming day, if the weather is warm enough”.

items.statement: Parents find the sports afternoons easier than the children do.
items.explanation: False — “some of them find [them] more intimidating than the children do”.

discussion: Caroline says children dislike being bad at something in public, not the activity itself. Is that true of adults as well?
Were teams picked in front of you at school? What did it feel like, and what would you have changed?
She designed a race that could not be won on speed alone. Is that fair to the fastest children?
“She kept the lesson and threw away the timetable.” Describe something that failed for you because of when, not what.
Write about 120 words about a teacher who changed how you felt about a subject, using the present perfect for what they have done and the past simple for one specific memory.
